summary.overview: A polypeptide folds into regular local shapes (secondary structure), packs these into a compact 3D form (tertiary structure) and may assemble with other chains (quaternary structure). Weak interactions plus disulfide bonds hold the native fold; chaperones help proteins fold, and misfolding causes disease.

sections.heading: Secondary structure
points: α-Helix: a right-handed coil with side chains pointing outwards, stabilised by backbone H-bonds between the C=O of residue n and the N–H of residue n + 4. It is the main structure in keratins.
Proline breaks helices, because of its rigid ring and its lack of an N–H.
β-Sheet: almost fully extended strands joined by backbone H-bonds between strands. Strands can be parallel (same N→C direction) or antiparallel; one chain can fold back on itself.
β-Turns: about four residues that reverse the chain's direction. Pro and Gly are common here.

sections.heading: Tertiary structure, domains and motifs
points: Tertiary structure is the full 3D fold of one chain; the primary structure determines it.
Globular proteins bury hydrophobic side chains inside and expose hydrophilic ones on the surface.
Motif (supersecondary structure): a recurring arrangement of helices and strands, found in many proteins.
Domain: an independently stable part of a chain, often with its own function (e.g. SH2 and SH3 domains for binding other proteins). A domain can contain several motifs.

sections.heading: Stabilising forces
points: Disulfide bonds (covalent, Cys–Cys) increase resistance to denaturation, especially in extracellular proteins.
The hydrophobic effect, from burying non-polar side chains, is the major driving force for folding.
Hydrogen bonds involve the backbone and polar side chains such as Ser, Thr, Asn and Gln.
Ionic interactions (salt bridges) form between Asp/Glu (–COO⁻) and Lys/Arg (–NH3⁺).

sections.heading: Quaternary structure
points: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits, which may be identical or different.
Subunits are held by non-covalent forces (H-bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions), e.g. haemoglobin α2β2.

sections.heading: Folding, denaturation and chaperones
points: Denaturation is loss of the native 3D shape; the sequence is unchanged. It can be reversible, but not always.

Causes: heat or radiation (break H-bonds, e.g. cooked egg white), strong acids or alkalis and high salt (break ionic bonds), heavy metals (bind carboxylates and precipitate proteins), and organic solvents and detergents (disrupt hydrophobic interactions; alcohol disinfects this way).
Chaperones help folding: Hsp70 binds nascent chains as they leave the ribosome; the Hsp60/Hsp10 chaperonin folds proteins inside its cavity using ATP.
Misfolded proteins are normally degraded. Some form insoluble amyloid fibres, as in Alzheimer's, Huntington's and Parkinson's diseases and in prion diseases such as scrapie and BSE.

keyTerms.definition: Coiled backbone stabilised by C=O(n)···H–N(n+4) hydrogen bonds.
Extended strands linked side by side by backbone hydrogen bonds; parallel or antiparallel.
Four-residue structure that reverses chain direction; often contains Pro or Gly.
Recurring supersecondary arrangement of helices and/or strands.
Independently stable folded unit of a polypeptide, often with a distinct function.
Loss of native 3D structure without breaking peptide bonds.
Protein that assists the folding of other proteins (e.g. Hsp70, Hsp60).
Insoluble fibrous aggregate of a misfolded protein.

examTips: α-Helix H-bonds run between backbone C=O and N–H, four residues apart; side chains point OUT.
Denaturation leaves the primary structure intact; peptide bonds break only under harsh, prolonged conditions.
The hydrophobic effect is the main driving force for folding; disulfides are the main COVALENT stabilisers.
Domain = independently stable unit; motif = recurring pattern of secondary elements.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O groups and N–H groups four residues further along
options.why: Every backbone C=O(n) bonds to N–H(n+4), with the side chains pointing outwards.

options.text: Disulfide bonds between neighbouring residues, which link each turn of the helix to the next
options.why: Disulfides are side-chain cross-links, not the basis of helices.

options.text: Ionic bonds between the side chains on adjacent strands, which hold the coil tightly together
options.why: Strands belong to β-sheets, and helix stability comes from backbone H-bonds.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between the side chains and the surrounding water molecules only
options.why: Helix H-bonds are internal to the backbone.

questions.stem: How does a β-sheet differ from an α-helix?

options.text: Its strands are almost fully extended and H-bond to neighbouring strands, parallel or antiparallel
options.why: In a sheet, the H-bonds run between strands rather than within a coil.

options.text: It has no hydrogen bonds at all and is held together by disulfide bonds between strands
options.why: All the backbone C=O and N–H groups take part in inter-strand H-bonds.

options.text: It can only form between two separate polypeptide chains, not within a single folded chain
options.why: A single chain can fold back on itself to form a sheet.

options.text: It is the main structure in α-keratin, where its extended strands give hair its great strength
options.why: α-Keratin is mostly α-helix; silk fibroin is rich in β-sheet.

questions.stem: Which two amino acids are especially common in β-turns?

options.text: Proline and glycine
options.why: Proline's kink and glycine's flexibility both suit tight turns that reverse chain direction.

options.text: Leucine and isoleucine
options.why: These bulky hydrophobic residues prefer helices and buried positions.

options.text: Lysine and arginine
options.why: These are not characteristic of turns.

options.text: Cysteine and methionine
options.why: Sulphur-containing residues are not typical turn residues.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a protein domain and a motif?

options.text: A domain is an independently stable folded unit; a motif is a recurring arrangement of secondary structure
options.why: A domain can contain several motifs and can move as a unit.

options.text: They are the same thing: both terms describe a region of a protein that binds a particular ligand
options.why: They describe different levels of organisation.

options.text: A motif is a whole folded protein, whereas a domain is a single amino acid within the active site
options.why: Motifs are a few secondary elements; domains are larger folded units.

options.text: Domains occur only in fibrous proteins, while motifs occur only in globular proteins such as enzymes
options.why: Domains are typical of globular proteins.

questions.stem: In a water-soluble globular protein, where are the polar and non-polar side chains usually found?

options.text: Non-polar side chains are buried inside; polar and charged side chains are on the surface
options.why: This arrangement maximises the hydrophobic effect and keeps the surface soluble.

options.text: Non-polar side chains are on the surface, and polar ones are buried inside to H-bond together
options.why: This would make the protein insoluble and unstable in water.

options.text: They are randomly distributed, because folding depends only on backbone hydrogen bonds
options.why: Folding sorts residues by polarity.

options.text: The side chains point into a central water channel that runs through the folded protein
options.why: Globular proteins are compact, with a dry hydrophobic core.

questions.stem: Which interaction is considered the main driving force for the folding of globular proteins?

options.text: The hydrophobic effect
options.why: Burying non-polar side chains releases ordered water, a large entropy gain.

options.text: Disulfide bonds
options.why: Disulfides stabilise the fold but form after it; many proteins have none.

options.text: Peptide bonds
options.why: Peptide bonds make the chain (primary structure), not the fold.

options.text: Covalent bonds to water
options.why: Water does not bond covalently to proteins during folding.

questions.stem: Many extracellular proteins, such as antibodies and digestive enzymes, contain several disulfide bonds. Why is this useful?

options.text: Covalent cross-links make the fold more resistant to denaturation outside the cell
options.why: Disulfides 'staple' parts of the chain together.

options.text: Disulfides make proteins positively charged, which keeps them soluble in the blood plasma
options.why: Disulfide bonds are uncharged.

options.text: Disulfides are the main force holding a protein together, so most proteins need them
options.why: Non-covalent forces dominate; disulfides add extra stability.

options.text: Disulfides form peptide bonds between subunits, joining them into a single polypeptide chain
options.why: Disulfides link Cys side chains; they are not peptide bonds.

questions.stem: A salt bridge in a protein is an interaction between which side chains?

options.text: A negatively charged Asp or Glu and a positively charged Lys or Arg
options.why: Opposite charges attract (ionic interaction).

options.text: Two cysteines, whose –SH groups are oxidised to form a bridge
options.why: Two cysteines form a covalent disulfide.

options.text: Two leucines, whose non-polar side chains pack against each other
options.why: Leucines interact hydrophobically.

options.text: Serine and water, sharing a hydrogen bond at the protein surface
options.why: This is an H-bond, not an ionic interaction.

questions.stem: Which statement about quaternary structure is correct?

options.text: It describes how two or more polypeptide subunits are arranged, held mainly by non-covalent forces
options.why: Example: haemoglobin's α2β2 tetramer.

options.text: Every protein has quaternary structure, even those that are made of only a single polypeptide chain
options.why: Monomeric proteins, such as myoglobin, have none.

options.text: Its subunits are joined end to end by peptide bonds, forming one long continuous chain
options.why: Subunits are separate chains, usually joined non-covalently.

options.text: It is another name for the amino acid sequence, read from the N-terminus to the C-terminus
options.why: That is primary structure.

questions.stem: When egg white is cooked, its proteins coagulate. What has happened at the molecular level?

options.text: Heat has disrupted weak bonds, so the proteins unfolded (denatured) and aggregated; the sequence is unchanged
options.why: Denaturation destroys 3D shape, not primary structure.

options.text: Heat has hydrolysed the peptide bonds into free amino acids, which then stick together as a solid
options.why: Normal cooking does not break peptide bonds.

options.text: New peptide bonds have formed between neighbouring proteins, joining them into one huge polymer
options.why: Aggregation is non-covalent, not peptide-bond formation.

options.text: The proteins have been converted into fats by the heat, which is why cooked egg white turns opaque
options.why: No chemical conversion to lipid occurs.

questions.stem: Why does 70% ethanol work as a skin disinfectant before an injection?

options.text: It disrupts hydrophobic interactions and H-bonding in bacterial proteins, denaturing them
options.why: Organic solvents unfold proteins, inactivating essential bacterial enzymes and structures.

options.text: It breaks bacterial DNA into free nucleotides, so the bacteria can no longer make proteins
options.why: Ethanol mainly acts on proteins and membranes.

options.text: It forms new disulfide bonds that lock bacterial proteins in place so that they cannot move
options.why: Ethanol is not an oxidant that creates disulfides.

options.text: It provides a nutrient that bacteria cannot digest, so they starve on the surface of the skin
options.why: Ethanol kills bacteria by denaturation, not starvation.

questions.stem: What is the role of the Hsp60/Hsp10 chaperonin system in mitochondria?

options.text: It encloses unfolded proteins in a cavity and helps them fold through repeated ATP-dependent cycles
options.why: Many mitochondrial proteins are imported unfolded and fold with chaperonin help.

options.text: It degrades newly made proteins so that only the correctly folded copies leave the ribosome
options.why: Chaperones aid folding; degradation is done by proteases and the proteasome.

options.text: It adds new peptide bonds to growing polypeptide chains as they enter the mitochondrial matrix
options.why: Peptide bonds are made by the ribosome.

options.text: It works without any energy input, using only the hydrophobic effect to pull the chains into shape
options.why: Chaperonin cycles require ATP.

questions.stem: Scrapie in sheep and BSE in cattle are caused by a normal cellular protein adopting an abnormal conformation. What does this illustrate?

options.text: A protein with an unchanged sequence can misfold into insoluble β-rich amyloid that damages tissue
options.why: Prion diseases, like Alzheimer's, are protein-misfolding disorders; the misfolded form converts normal copies.

options.text: These diseases are caused by a change in the protein's primary structure, as in sickle-cell disease
options.why: In infectious prion disease the sequence is the same; the conformation differs.

options.text: Misfolded proteins are degraded harmlessly, so the damage comes from a separate virus
options.why: Amyloid aggregates resist degradation and accumulate.

options.text: The proteins are denatured into random coils by the heat of the brain, so they lose their function
options.why: The abnormal form is a different, highly ordered aggregate.

questions.stem: Heavy-metal ions such as Pb²⁺ and Hg²⁺ are toxic partly because of their effect on proteins. What do they do?

options.text: They bind carboxylate and thiol side chains, disrupting ionic interactions so that proteins precipitate
options.why: Denaturation and precipitation inactivate enzymes.

options.text: They hydrolyse the peptide bonds in the protein, breaking it down into its free amino acids
options.why: They act on side-chain interactions, not the backbone.

options.text: They act as chaperones that refold proteins into abnormal shapes that the cell cannot use
options.why: They disrupt, rather than assist, folding.

options.text: They increase protein solubility so much that proteins leak out of cells and are lost in urine
options.why: They reduce net charge and solubility.

questions.stem: A purified enzyme is fully unfolded with urea and its disulfides reduced. After slowly removing the urea and re-oxidising, full activity returns. What does this show?

options.text: All the information needed for the native 3D fold is contained in the amino acid sequence
options.why: This classic experiment (Anfinsen, ribonuclease) showed that primary structure determines tertiary structure.

options.text: Urea creates new peptide bonds as it is removed, rebuilding the enzyme's active site
options.why: Urea disrupts non-covalent interactions; it makes no peptide bonds.

options.text: Chaperones are always essential for folding, so some must have been present in the sample
options.why: This protein refolded without chaperones (though many proteins in cells need help).

options.text: Denaturation always permanently destroys proteins, so the enzyme must have been re-made
options.why: Here denaturation was reversible.

flashcards.front: α-Helix: H-bond pattern and side-chain direction?
flashcards.back: Backbone H-bonds: C=O of residue n to N–H of residue n + 4. Side chains point outwards; Pro breaks helices.
Parallel: all strands run N→C in the same direction. Antiparallel: neighbouring strands alternate. Both are H-bonded between strands.
About four residues that reverse chain direction; often contains Pro and Gly.
Domain: independently stable unit, often with its own function. Motif: recurring arrangement of helices and strands (supersecondary structure).
Disulfide bonds (covalent), hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions (salt bridges).
Arrangement of two or more subunits, held by non-covalent forces, e.g. haemoglobin α2β2.
Loss of native 3D shape with the sequence unchanged. Sometimes reversible (renaturation).

flashcards.front: Denaturing agents and what they disrupt?
flashcards.back: Heat or radiation: H-bonds. Strong acid or alkali and high salt: ionic bonds. Heavy metals: bind carboxylates and thiols. Organic solvents and detergents: hydrophobic interactions.
Hsp70: binds nascent chains leaving the ribosome to prevent premature folding. Hsp60/10: chaperonin cavity that folds proteins using ATP (e.g. in mitochondria).
Alzheimer's, Huntington's and Parkinson's diseases (amyloid fibres); prion diseases such as scrapie and BSE.
